scenario: Legal asks whether customers' messages to the planned shopping assistant could be used to train someone else's model, and where they are processed.
options: OpenAI's public API with a company card instead of a personal one
An Azure OpenAI deployment in the company's subscription, on a Data Zone (EU) deployment type, where prompts and outputs are not used for training
Any model, as long as the system prompt tells it not to store data
A Global Standard deployment, because it has the most quota
explanation: Azure's contract excludes training on your data, and a Data Zone deployment keeps processing inside the EU. A system prompt cannot change where data goes, and Global Standard may process requests in any region.

stem: What is the best rule for choosing a model for a new task?
options: Use the largest model available, so quality is never the problem
Use a reasoning model for everything, since it thinks harder
Fine-tune a model first, then choose a size
Start with the smallest model that passes your evaluation, and move up only where it fails
explanation: Flagship and reasoning models cost many times more per token and are slower. Many tasks, such as extraction, classification and short drafting, pass evaluation on a small model, and you only know that by testing.

scenario: A job generating 40,000 descriptions fails after 2,000 with HTTP 429 errors.
stem: What is the right first response?
options: Retry with backoff that honours retry-after, and move the bulk job to a Batch deployment; raise quota only if real usage needs it
Switch to the largest model, because it has more capacity
Buy provisioned throughput units immediately
Run the job from several laptops in parallel
explanation: A 429 means the deployment's tokens-per-minute share is used up. Well-behaved retries and a half-price batch deployment suit a job that can wait. PTUs are for steady, heavy traffic, and parallel laptops just hit the same quota faster.

stem: Why does each message in a long chat cost more than the one before?
options: Azure charges a premium for long sessions
The model stores the conversation and bills for storage
The model is stateless, so the app resends the whole history on each turn, and every resent token is billed again
Output tokens get more expensive as the conversation goes on
explanation: Chat 'memory' is the app resending history. Trimming or summarising older turns keeps both the cost and the context size under control.

scenario: Two workloads: a nightly job rewriting product descriptions from supplier data, and a live assistant where customers type their names and addresses.
options: Provisioned for both, for predictable latency
Regional Standard for the job, and Global Standard for the assistant for the highest quota
Global Standard for both
Global Batch for the job, since it can wait and holds no personal data; Data Zone Standard for the assistant, to keep personal data in the chosen zone
explanation: Batch costs about half as much and suits work that can wait up to a day. Personal data belongs on a Data Zone or regional type. Global Standard for the assistant would let requests be processed anywhere in the world.

scenario: Ana proposes fine-tuning a model on the product catalogue so the assistant 'knows' every product.
options: Fine-tuning is not available on Azure
Fine-tuning teaches style and format, not reliable facts. The catalogue changes weekly, so the model would be stale and still invent details. Retrieving current product data is the right tool.
Fine-tuned models cannot use a system prompt
It would make the model larger and slower
explanation: Facts belong in retrieval, which is always current and can be cited. Fine-tuning helps with a consistent style or a narrow format. It also adds training and hourly hosting costs.

stem: When do provisioned throughput units (PTUs) make sense?
options: Steady, heavy traffic that needs predictable latency, where reserved capacity costs less than the same tokens pay-as-you-go
Any new prototype, to avoid 429 errors
Bulk jobs that can wait 24 hours
Whenever data must stay in the EU
explanation: PTUs are paid for whether they are used or not, so they suit a steady baseline, often with overflow spilling to a Standard deployment. Bulk work belongs on Batch, and residency comes from the deployment type, which exists for both pay-per-token and provisioned deployments.

stem: A model offers a context window of a million tokens. What should the team conclude?
options: The whole catalogue and all customer history can go into every prompt at no extra cost
Retrieval is no longer needed
Every token sent is billed on every call, and material in the middle of long prompts gets less attention, so send only what the task needs
Output length is now unlimited
explanation: A large window is a limit, not free memory. Stuffing it raises cost and latency and can lower quality. Retrieval that selects the few relevant passages usually does better.
